title: Directive Principles — meaning and constitutional purpose

content.overview: Part IV of the Constitution sets out Directive Principles of State Policy. They guide the State toward a social order based on justice — social, economic and political. They are not enforceable as fundamental rights in court, but Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country.

sections.heading: Constitutional placement
sections.body: Part IV follows Part III (Fundamental Rights). Article 36 adopts the Part III meaning of 'the State'. Article 37 states that the principles are not enforceable by any court, yet are fundamental in governance and that it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. Verify exact wording against the official Constitution text on India Code / Legislative Department editions.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.body: Directive Principles articulate policy goals: welfare, social and economic justice, decentralisation, labour standards, environment, and international peace. They inform legislation, executive policy, and — within limits fixed by judicial doctrine — constitutional interpretation of Part III.

sections.heading: Track B — pleading
sections.body: Do not frame a pure Part IV claim as if it were an Article 32 right. Use implementing statutes, schemes, and Part III standards (especially Articles 14, 19 and 21) where a justiciable right is asserted. Cite the Directive Principle to explain legislative purpose or reasonableness where doctrine permits.

sections.heading: Historical note
sections.body: The Directive Principles draw on the idea of non-justiciable policy directives. Indian judicial history moved from a stricter separation of Parts III and IV toward harmonisation, subject always to the text of Article 37 and to later decisions on Article 31C and basic structure. Distinguish historical case outcomes from the present constitutional text.
